opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't that I thought big-company research was bad. Those labs have incredible resources and very smart people. But when I thought about what I wanted to spend the next ten or twenty years doing, I realized it didn't quite fit.

The first issue is ownership of the problem. In a large company, even in a research lab, the direction ultimately has to align with the company's product roadmap and business priorities. That's reasonable, since they're paying for it. But it means you're often optimizing someone else's question. The problem I cared about, getting robots to actually understand and act in the physical world, needed a long, focused, end-to-end effort. I wasn't sure a big company would let me pursue that in the way I believed was right, especially in the early days when it looked risky and unfashionable.

The second issue is the distance between research and reality. At a big company you can publish great papers, but whether your work becomes a real system that people use often depends on many layers of decisions you don't control. I wanted a tighter loop, where you build the hardware, the data pipeline, and the models, put them in the real world, see them fail, and fix them. That loop is where I think the real progress in embodied intelligence happens.

The third reason is more personal. I felt there was a window, both in the technology and in China's ecosystem, where you could build something from scratch, train your own team, and shape the field instead of being one contributor among thousands. Hardware supply chains, manufacturing capability, and a generation of very hungry young researchers were all there. Joining a big U.S. lab would have been a comfortable, respectable path, but I would always have wondered what would have happened if I had tried to build it myself.

So it was less "that path is unattractive" and more "this other path is the one I couldn't forgive myself for not taking."

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't that it was a bad path. For a lot of people it's a great path. I just felt, after a few years in those environments, that I could see the next ten years very clearly, and that clarity scared me more than it comforted me.

In a big American lab, you're one of thousands of researchers. The resources are incredible, the colleagues are brilliant, but the direction is set far above you. You publish papers, you push a benchmark, maybe a piece of your work gets folded into a product two years later, and you rarely get to see the whole loop. You don't decide what problem matters. You're optimizing a small slice of a very large machine.

And I kept noticing that the questions I actually cared about, the ones that kept me up at night, weren't the ones that got prioritized. They were too early, too risky, too far from the current roadmap. At a big company, "interesting" has to fight against "safe," and safe usually wins.

There was also a timing element. I felt that this was a once-in-a-generation moment for AI, and the window for small teams to do something that matters is open right now. In five years it may be closed. If I'm going to take a risk, this is the time to do it, not when I'm fifty and have a mortgage and a very comfortable title.

And then there's the more personal part. I grew up in China, I studied there, and a lot of the people I want to build with are there. I wanted to be in an environment where I could set the agenda, build a team from scratch, and be responsible for the outcome, good or bad. That ownership is what I was missing. A research job at a big company gives you stability and prestige, but it doesn't give you that.

So it's not that I thought the path was wrong. I just thought it wasn't mine.
